Search results point to Better Auth as the usual pick for new Next.js projects in 2026, with Clerk and Auth.js in narrower roles. The sources are mostly vendor-adjacent blogs, and a few results were spam pages with no useful content.

- **Better Auth:** It's a self-hosted TypeScript library that keeps users and sessions in your own database. It launched in 2024 and reached v1.6 in May 2026. One comparison says it offers the most complete built-in feature set, including 2FA, passkeys, and RBAC, but its maintenance burden falls on your team (Self-managed — you're responsible for security updates).
- **Auth.js (formerly NextAuth):** Several sources describe it as a legacy choice now. As of September 2025, the Better Auth team took over Auth.js maintenance, and the library is in security-patch mode. Existing Auth.js v5 apps keep working, but starting a new project on it means betting on a library its own maintainers steer users away from.
- **Clerk:** It's a hosted service with prebuilt UI. Its cost is the main objection. One source lists Pro $25/mo + $0.02/MRU over 50k pricing, and another says it gets expensive past 50,000 MAU and locks your user data in a US database. The tradeoff is that the session store, user database, and JWT signing keys all live in Clerk's infrastructure.
- **Supabase Auth (not asked about, but mentioned):** It's the other frequently recommended option, mainly if you already use Supabase, because Row Level Security can do half your authorization work.

**Bottom line:** Sources lean toward Better Auth for new projects that want control and no per-user fees. Clerk suits teams that want managed auth and polished UI and accept usage-based pricing. Auth.js is mainly for existing apps. Treat the pricing and feature claims as vendor-blog claims and check current pricing directly.

title: proxy.js
description: API reference for the proxy.js file.
related:
  title: Learn more about Proxy
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/next-request
    - app/api-reference/functions/next-response
---

> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.

The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.

Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.

> **Good to know**:
>
> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
>
> To pass information from Proxy to your application, use [headers](#setting-headers), [cookies](#using-cookies), [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#rewrite), [redirects](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#redirect), or the URL.

Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.

If you’ve customized [`pageExtensions`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions), for example to `.page.ts` or `.page.js`, name your file `proxy.page.ts` or `proxy.page.js` accordingly.

```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'

// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
}

export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
}
```

```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'

// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
export function proxy(request) {
  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
}

export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
}
```

## Exports

### Proxy function

The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.

content.text:
Everything is verified end to end; I'm wrapping up with a summary.

Auth is in: email/password sign up and sign in, Google sign-in, and `/dashboard` only reachable when signed in. I ran it against a production build. These cases passed:
- Anonymous `/dashboard` gets a 307 redirect to `/sign-in`.
- Sign-up returns 200, and the dashboard then shows the new user.
- Sign-in works with the right password (200) and fails with a wrong one (401).
- The Google flow generates a redirect URL to Google's OAuth page. I didn't complete a real Google login, since the credentials are placeholders.

`npm run lint` is clean. `tsc` reports `LayoutProps` as missing in `layout.tsx`, which this change didn't touch, and `next build` succeeds.

**Choice: [Better Auth](https://supastarter.dev/blog/better-auth-vs-nextauth-vs-clerk)** with a local SQLite file via `better-sqlite3`.
- Better Auth is self-hosted, has email/password and Google built in, and has no per-user fees. Comparison write-ups such as [Makerkit's](https://makerkit.dev/blog/tutorials/better-auth-vs-clerk) lean toward it for new Next.js projects, though those are mostly vendor-adjacent blogs.
- Auth.js is described as security-patch-only now that the Better Auth team has taken over its maintenance. I skipped it for a new project.
- Clerk is hosted, with usage-based pricing and your user data on their servers. I skipped it for those reasons.

**What changed:**
- **Server and client setup:** `src/lib/auth.ts`, `src/lib/auth-client.ts` and `src/app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts`.
- **Route protection:** `src/proxy.ts` (Next 16 renamed middleware to proxy) redirects to `/sign-in` when there's no session cookie. That check only looks at the cookie, so the dashboard page also validates the session and redirects if it's invalid.
- **`src/lib/users.ts`:** `getCurrentUser()` now reads the real session. `listUsers()` and `getUser()` read Better Auth's `user` table. The `User` type and function signatures are unchanged.
- **Pages:** `/sign-in` and `/sign-up` (shared form in `src/components/auth-form.tsx`), plus a sign-out button on the dashboard.
- **Config:** `.env.example` holds placeholder credentials. I added `!.env.example` and `*.db` to `.gitignore`, because the existing `.env*` rule would have ignored the example file.

**What to know:**
- The hardcoded Ada and Grace users are gone. They had no credentials, so the Team list starts empty until people sign up.
- To run it:
  1. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local`. I created one with the placeholders, and it's gitignored.
  2. Fill in real values, including a real `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`.
  3. Run `npx @better-auth/cli@latest migrate -y` to create the tables.
  4. Add `http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/google` as the redirect URI in your Google OAuth client.
- `BETTER_AUTH_URL` must match the origin you browse from. Requests from another port return `INVALID_ORIGIN`, which I hit when I first tested on port 3111.
- SQLite on a local file won't work on serverless hosts such as Vercel. For those, switch the `database` option in `src/lib/auth.ts` to Postgres.
- Nothing is committed.
